title: eBPF-assisted tail detection to remove hot-path tracer allocations
creator: Marcos Ortega
description:
Background: We've observed a recurring pattern where tail trace sampling (to capture rare high-latency requests) imposes allocations and lock contention on the hot request path. Several recent perf regressions correlate with tracer allocations in the ingress SDK; while tail sampling is valuable for debugging, the cost at 1P+ QPS services is non-trivial. Existing mitigations (deferred async commit, reservoir samplers) lower overhead but still require touching request-scoped data structures in the hot path, which leads to allocation spikes under load.

Proposal: Implement a lightweight kernel-level signal for tail candidates using eBPF-based latency probes. The idea is to detect long-running requests without allocating or locking in the hot path. When latency crosses a short threshold (e.g., 80th/95th percentile cutoff or absolute ms), eBPF writes a compact record to a ring buffer consumed by a low-priority background process. That background process will trigger the full tracing and KV-cache capture for that request (or signal the SDK to mark the trace) out of band. This keeps the hot path zero-allocation and avoids tracer mutexes while preserving tail-sample fidelity.

Goals / Acceptance Criteria:
- Hot-path CPU and allocation overhead from tracing hooks reduced to <0.5% at p95 load compared to baseline.
- Tail capture fidelity: >=95% of previously-captured long-tail traces remain capturable for the same threshold.
- No increase in end-to-end 99th percentile latency due to sampling instrumentation.
- Safe by default: non-root fallback to user-space sampling with a clear runtime flag.

Design details and trade-offs:
- eBPF approach pros: zero-allocation hot path, low-latency detection, composable with existing kernel observability features.
- eBPF cons: requires elevated privileges in some environments (Private deployments/on-prem), portability variations across kernels. To address this we provide a fallback user-space detector that uses a very cheap watermark timer (clock_gettime + non-allocating atomic update).
- Privacy/security: eBPF consumer only records request IDs and timing markers. Payloads (headers, bodies) are captured only by the background process running in user-space, preserving existing PII redaction steps. Security review flagged potential eBPF attack surface; we limit maps and use read-only program load policies.
- Operational complexity: we add a small agent daemon (observability-sidecar) to the existing infra images for Dedicated/Private. Hosted mode will run the eBPF on our managed instances with tighter controls.

Implementation plan (phases):
1) Spike + PoC (done): simple eBPF kprobe on accept/read loop + ring buffer to user-space consumer. PoC shows detection without allocations and 40-60% reduction in hot-path CPU for synthetic load. See notes: https://confluence.internal.redwood.com/display/OBS/EBPF-Tail-Detector-POC
2) Instrumentation hardening (current): extend PoC to record per-request trace ID (32B) and a compact state (flags) into ring buffer; implement robust consumer with backpressure and rate-limiting.
3) SDK integration: consumer writes a marker to the SDK tracer via a light IPC (unix domain socket) to request full trace capture; SDK performs capture asynchronously. Add opt-in runtime config.
4) Canary & rollout: run on staging, then a small fleet of low-traffic production services, monitor overhead dashboards and error rates.

Progress updates (timeline):
- 2026-03-02: Engineering spike started (Samir + Leah).
- 2026-03-06: PoC validated on k8s-staging; synthetic benchmark shows hot-path allocation drop from 12MB/s to 0.8MB/s and CPU drop of ~0.5 -> 0.28 per-core at p95.
- 2026-03-10: Formal ticket created (this doc).
- 2026-03-11: Integration prototype committed: https://github.com/redwood/observability-agent/pull/6789 (DO NOT MERGE).
- 2026-03-12: Security review kickoff; initial feedback expects a scoped RBAC and LSM-compatible policy.

Open decisions / trade-offs: 
- Thresholding model: use a static absolute ms threshold (e.g., 200ms) vs adaptive percentile-based detection. Adaptive percentiles require short-term sliding windows in the agent and complicate eBPF-only detection. Decision: implement absolute threshold first (configurable), iterate to percentile detector in phase 2.
- Fallback behavior for Private customers that disallow eBPF: default to the user-space watermark detector and flag in console UI that tail fidelity may be reduced.

Code/patch links:
- PoC branch: https://github.com/redwood/observability-agent/tree/feature/ebpf-tail-poc
- WIP consumer + SDK IPC: https://github.com/redwood/observability-agent/pull/6789
- Design doc and benchmarks: https://confluence.internal.redwood.com/display/OBS/EBPF-Tail-Detector-Design

Review feedback (notes):
- Security (A. Nair): require signed eBPF blobs and restrict map sizes; add read-only mode for Hosted.
- Platform (J. Rivera): prefer to ship agent as an opt-in sidecar for Dedicated customers; hosted instances will have it enabled behind a feature flag.
- Observability (P. Huang): request dashboards instrumenting ring buffer drop rates and consumer lag; added dashboards to staging: https://grafana.internal.redwood.com/d/ebpf-tail/agent-health

Next steps / checklist:
- [ ] Harden ring buffer handling and implement consumer backpressure (in progress).
- [ ] Implement SDK IPC API and minimal capture handshake (in progress).
- [ ] Add RBAC + signed eBPF artifacts to CI (blocked by security review).
- [ ] Create canary plan and alerting thresholds (SLO changes, allocation/CPU regressions).
- [ ] Run 2-week staging soak with real traffic and evaluate capture fidelity metrics.

Canary and rollout plan:
- Canary group: small set of services serving non-critical workloads (payment-ingress fallback off).
- Metrics to watch: ring_buffer_drop_rate, consumer_lag_ms, hotpath_allocs_per_sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, trace_capture_rate, error_budget_burn.
- Rollout gates: if hotpath CPU/alloc increases >2% or ring buffer drop >1%, rollback agent.

Rollback & mitigation: agent toggles are feature-flagged; if we see adverse effects, we will flip eBPF -> user-space detector and push a quick agent rollback.

Follow-ups (post-launch):
- Evaluate moving detection logic into kernel sampling maps for even lower overhead.
- Explore enriching event data for automated debugging (stack-unwinding in kernel not allowed; continue user-space capture).
- Consider marketplace/private deployment docs and installer perms.

Notes: This ticket is intentionally conservative in scope to avoid touching hotpath SDK allocations directly and to provide a cross-environment fallback. Coordination required with Security, Platform, and DevEx for customer docs and flags.
